Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

the adjective

the definite article

also the one who, the famous

classical

Quint. 1.4.19: noster sermō articulōs nōn dēsīderat

nōmen sine articulō

Latin has no article

no word: the noun alone

English “the” is not translated: “the countryman waits for the river to run out” is rūsticus exspectat dum dēfluat amnis. Where it matters which one is meant, Latin says so with a pronoun (below); otherwise the context decides.

Other words

  • ille, illa, illud (after its noun) — the famous, the well-known

    demonstrative, after a name or noun · also used · classical · Cic. Imp. Pomp. 22: Mēdēa illa (Lewis & Short); Cic. Sen. 50: honestum illud Solōnis est (Lewis & Short)

    The “the” of something everyone knows: Xenophōn, Sōcraticus ille, Xenophon, the pupil of Socrates (Cic. de Or. 2.58, Lewis & Short).

  • is, ea, id … quī — the one who, the … that

    is with a relative clause · also used · classical · Cic. Amic. 80: is quī est tamquam alter īdem; Hor. Epod. 2.1: beātus ille quī procul negōtiīs

    “The man who”, “the thing that”: is quī, id quod; with more weight, ille quī.

Examples

  • rūsticus exspectat dum dēfluat amnis; at ille lābitur et lābētur in omne volūbilis aevum

    the countryman waits for the river to run out; but on it glides, and will glide, rolling on for everHor. Ep. 1.2.42–43

  • pendentem summā capream dē rūpe vidēbis: cāsūram spērēs; dēspicit illa canēs

    you will see the goat hanging from the top of the cliff; you would expect it to fall; it looks down on the dogsMart. 13.98.1–2

  • beātus ille quī procul negōtiīs, ut prīsca gēns mortālium

    happy the man who, far from business, like the first race of men …Hor. Epod. 2.1–2

  • noster sermō articulōs nōn dēsīderat

    our language has no need of articlesQuint. 1.4.19

See also a, that, which.
